title: Deployment Basics
subtitle: npm scripts, health endpoints, process managers, and Docker basics for Node.js
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Running `node index.js` works locally but isn't suitable for production: the process dies on errors, doesn't restart automatically, doesn't scale across CPU cores, and has no way for monitoring tools to check if it's healthy.
whyItExists.solution: npm scripts standardize commands. A /health endpoint lets load balancers verify the app is running. Process managers (PM2) keep the app running, restart on crash, and manage logs. Docker packages the app and its runtime so it runs identically anywhere.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any Node.js application you intend to run in production — hosted VPS, Docker container, cloud run service, or PaaS like Railway/Render.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For serverless deployments (Vercel, Netlify Functions, AWS Lambda), the platform manages the process — you don't need PM2. But health endpoints and npm scripts are still valuable.

explainModes.beginner: Deployment means running your Node.js app in a way that keeps it running reliably. The key steps: use npm start as the command to run your app (defined in package.json scripts), add a /health route that returns 200 OK so load balancers can check it's alive, and use a process manager like PM2 so the app restarts automatically if it crashes.
explainModes.simple: package.json scripts: 'start' runs the production server, 'dev' runs with nodemon for auto-reload, 'build' compiles TypeScript. process.env.PORT: always listen on the port from environment (hosting platforms set this). Health endpoint: GET /health returns { status: 'ok', uptime: process.uptime() }. PM2: npm install -g pm2, pm2 start index.js, pm2 logs, pm2 restart, pm2 startup (auto-start on reboot). Graceful shutdown: listen for SIGTERM, stop accepting requests, wait for in-flight requests, close DB connections, exit.
explainModes.standard: Dockerfile structure: FROM node:20-alpine (small base), WORKDIR /app, COPY package*.json ./ (separate layer for cache), RUN npm ci --production (install only prod deps), COPY . . (source after deps for cache), CMD ['node', 'index.js']. .dockerignore: node_modules, .env, .git, *.log. Multi-stage build: separate build stage (compiles TypeScript) from runtime stage (only compiled output). EXPOSE port in Dockerfile is documentation — you still need -p flag when running. Environment vars: docker run -e NODE_ENV=production --env-file .env.production.
explainModes.technical: node --max-old-space-size=512: limit Node heap size for container memory limit. Cluster module: fork one worker per CPU core — each handles requests independently. PM2 cluster mode: pm2 start index.js -i max (spawns #CPU workers automatically). Zero-downtime restart: pm2 reload (workers restart one at a time — no dropped connections). Docker health check: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost:$PORT/health || exit 1. kubernetes readiness/liveness probes: readiness hits /ready (app warmed up), liveness hits /health (process alive).
explainModes.deepDive: 12-factor app: a methodology for production-ready apps. Key factors relevant to Node.js: III (config via env vars, not code), IV (npm scripts as process types), VII (port binding — app is self-contained), XI (logs as event stream to stdout — no log files in app). Graceful shutdown pattern: server.close(callback) stops accepting new connections but waits for existing requests to finish. Track in-flight requests manually or use terminus / stoppable packages. Container signals: Docker sends SIGTERM to PID 1 on stop. Node.js must be PID 1 (not a shell) to receive it — use exec form CMD ['node', 'index.js'], not shell form CMD node index.js.

content.code:
# Build stage — compile TypeScript (omit if using plain JS)
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage — lean production image
FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Install only production dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --production && npm cache clean --force

# Copy compiled output from build stage
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

# Non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

EXPOSE 3000

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=5s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

# exec form — makes Node PID 1 so it receives signals
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

content.text: Always listen on `process.env.PORT || 3000` — never hardcode a port. Every major hosting platform (Railway, Render, Heroku, Fly.io) sets PORT automatically. If you hardcode a port, your app won't start.

questions.question: Why should a Dockerfile use CMD ["node", "index.js"] (exec form) instead of CMD node index.js (shell form)?
options: Exec form is faster because it skips the shell startup overhead
Exec form makes Node.js PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM directly from Docker. Shell form makes the shell PID 1 — it may not forward signals to Node, preventing graceful shutdown.
Shell form only works on Linux; exec form is cross-platform
questions.explanation: When Docker stops a container, it sends SIGTERM to PID 1. In exec form ["node", "index.js"], Node.js is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly — your process.on('SIGTERM', gracefulShutdown) handler runs. In shell form `node index.js`, the shell (/bin/sh) is PID 1. The shell may or may not forward signals to its child process (Node). If it doesn't forward SIGTERM, Docker waits 10 seconds (the default grace period) and then sends SIGKILL — your graceful shutdown never runs and in-flight requests are dropped.

faq.q: What's the simplest way to deploy a Node.js app to production?
faq.a: For the simplest path: use Railway or Render. Connect your GitHub repo, they detect Node.js automatically, run `npm start`, and set PORT for you. Add a /health endpoint and you're done. For more control, use a VPS (DigitalOcean Droplet, Linode) with PM2: `pm2 start npm -- start`, `pm2 startup` (survives reboot), `pm2 save`. For containerized deployments, build a Docker image and push to a registry, then run it anywhere (Railway, Fly.io, Google Cloud Run, AWS ECS).
